publication.title: Energix Brings 152 MW Ohio Solar Farm Online With Stem Controls

article.raw_gutenberg:
Energix US has brought its Border Basin Solar facility in Hancock County, Ohio, into operation, adding 152 megawatts of direct-current solar panels and 120 megawatts of alternating-current capacity to the PJM electricity market. Stem confirmed the commissioning in a November 3, 2026 announcement, identifying its PowerTrack platform as the plant's control and monitoring system. The project is operational, rather than another proposed capacity addition.

How does utility-scale solar work? Photovoltaic modules turn sunlight into direct-current electricity. Inverters convert the output into alternating current suitable for transmission and grid use. A plant controller coordinates the inverters, follows grid-operator instructions and monitors power quality, while a supervisory control and data acquisition system, or SCADA, collects equipment measurements and alarms. Those controls matter because large solar sites must operate as coordinated power stations, not merely collections of panels.

Border Basin's 152 MWdc / 120 MWac ratings imply a DC-to-AC capacity ratio of approximately 1.27. Developers commonly install more panel nameplate capacity than inverter output capacity to improve utilization during lower-irradiance hours. Under strong sun, conversion limits can constrain instantaneous AC output, a behavior called clipping. Neither rating represents an observed daily energy yield: actual electricity generation is measured in megawatt-hours and varies with weather, availability and curtailment. BitcoinVersus.Tech previously documented long-term renewable capacity growth, where the same distinction applies.

Stem's contribution included engineering, panel-shop preparation, factory acceptance testing, field commissioning, utility witness testing and operator handoff. At the operational site, PowerTrack integrates plant controls, local SCADA, communications equipment, weather stations and a connection to PJM's network. Cloud software adds performance reports, notifications, analytics and remote backup. The release does not quantify a reduction in operating costs or provide independently measured increases in solar output attributable to the software.

The plant also illustrates why software-driven controls have become part of renewable infrastructure. Weather readings can be compared with electrical output to flag equipment behavior, while control signals help operators stay within grid requirements. Yet remote monitoring introduces cybersecurity, data-quality and communications-dependency considerations. Comparable monitoring principles appear in BitcoinVersus.Tech's guide to networking, switches and power-distribution monitoring; the report does not claim Border Basin specifically uses SNMP.

Energix says its operational U.S. portfolio in the PJM market now exceeds 1 gigawatt after the Border Basin milestone. That company-reported portfolio figure is distinct from the output of the single Ohio facility. The development occurs as grid operators consider rising demand from large industrial and computing loads. BitcoinVersus.Tech has reported on PJM's data-center connection and reliability rules and why new power lines can take longer than renewable projects to complete.

Solar energy's variable output also shapes decisions about storage. A battery can shift electricity from sunny periods to later demand, but Stem's November announcement does not identify an operating battery at Border Basin. Storage additions elsewhere are documented in BitcoinVersus.Tech's review of U.S. solar-plus-battery development. The absence of disclosed battery specifications prevents claims about Border Basin's nighttime delivery capability.

The next meaningful evidence will be recorded energy production, capacity factors, grid curtailment, equipment availability and operating costs over successive seasons. Independently published operating data would also clarify whether the site's control and analytics stack delivers measurable improvements. For now, Energix has confirmed a completed generation asset, while Stem has documented the software and hardware infrastructure used to manage its performance.
